Characterized by erythema nodosum (1 mark) — Coccidioides immitis / Histoplasma capsulatum

Sarcoidosis: non-caseating granulomas; young adults; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with or without parenchymal disease; erythema nodosum, arthralgia, uveitis, hypercalcaemia, raised ACE; Löfgren syndrome (bilateral hilar nodes + erythema nodosum + arthralgia, good prognosis).
A young woman has erythema nodosum, arthralgia and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
| Sarcoidosis | Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, multi-system | Non-caseating granulomas on biopsy, elevated ACE |

Skin: *Lesions (ulcers, pustules, necrotic eschars), cellulitis, erythema nodosum?* — Necrotic eschar → cutaneous anthrax; cellulitis → Staphylococcus/Streptococcus; erythema nodosum → TB or sarcoidosis.
Skin – erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum: Immune‑mediated extra‑intestinal manifestations; help differentiate from infection.
| Sarcoidosis | Bilateral hilar nodes, erythema nodosum | Non-caseating granulomas |

qs.q: A young adult under 40 years old presents with erythema nodosum, peripheral arthropathy, uveitis, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of this multisystem disorder?
o: IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to occupational organic dusts
Autoantibody production against type IV collagen in the membrane
Direct bacterial infection of the alveolar walls by tuberculosis
Abnormal CD4 mediated cell reaction to an unknown antigen
qs.e: Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating granulomatous inflammation driven by an abnormal CD4-mediated cell reaction to an unknown antigen. It is not caused by active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection despite forming granulomas.

qs.q: A 32-year-old man presents with erythema nodosum, peripheral arthropathy, uveitis, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations reveal hypercalcemia. Which of the following is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for the hypercalcemia in this multisystem granulomatous disorder?
o: Excessive dietary calcium absorption via altered gut mucosa
Increased formation of calcitriol by alveolar macrophages
Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid gland receptors
Direct destruction of bony trabeculae by systemic granulomas
qs.e: Hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis occurs due to increased formation of calcitriol by the alveolar macrophages. It is not caused by direct bone destruction or parathyroid receptor autoimmunity.

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage 1 sarcoidosis after presenting with erythema nodosum and arthralgia. She has no pulmonary symptoms. What is the typical natural history of stage 1 sarcoidosis?
o: Transforms rapidly into a malignant pulmonary neoplasm
Always progresses inevitably to ventilatory failure
qs.e: Stage 1 sarcoidosis is often asymptomatic or presents with erythema nodosum and arthralgia, and can resolve spontaneously within 1 year. Progression to ventilatory failure is characteristic of much more advanced stages.

o: Hallmark of acute sarcoidosis — raised tender nodules on anterior legs
Subcutaneous sarcoid nodules with abundant granulomas
Chronic skin infiltration by noncaseating granulomas
Cutaneous sarcoid granulomas on the legs

es.q: A patient diagnosed with sarcoidosis presents with hypercalcemia and erythema nodosum. Explain the underlying mechanisms for these two associated clinical features of sarcoidosis.
es.m: 1. **Hypercalcemia**: In sarcoidosis, hypercalcemia is caused by the active production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (the active form of Vitamin D) by macrophages within the noncaseating granulomas. These activated macrophages possess the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, leading to increased intestinal absorption of calcium and subsequent hypercalcemia. 2. **Erythema Nodosum**: This is a common skin sign associated with acute sarcoidosis. Erythema nodosum is characterized by tender, red nodules, typically on the shins, and is a form of panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat). es.q: A 35-year-old female presents with fatigue, cough, and erythema nodosum. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. What is the likely diagnosis, what is the characteristic histological finding, and what is the underlying mechanism for hypercalcemia if present in this condition?
es.m: 1. **Likely Diagnosis:** The likely diagnosis is Sarcoidosis, given the clinical presentation of erythema nodosum (a skin sign of acute sarcoidosis) and the histological finding of noncaseating granulomas. 2. **Characteristic Histological Finding:** The hallmark histological feature of sarcoidosis is the presence of noncaseating granulomas in multiple organs. Diagnosis is typically one of exclusion, after ruling out other causes of granulomatous disease. 3. **Mechanism of Hypercalcemia:** If hypercalcemia is present in sarcoidosis, it is caused by active Vitamin D production by activated macrophages within the granulomas. es.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with constitutional symptoms, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and skin lesions (erythema nodosum). A biopsy reveals noncaseating granulomas. Explain the characteristic histological finding for this condition and describe the mechanism behind the hypercalcemia sometime
es.m: The characteristic histological finding for this condition (Sarcoidosis) is the presence of **noncaseating granulomas** in multiple organs. Hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis is caused by **active Vitamin D production by macrophages within the granulomas**. These activated macrophages convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption and subsequent hypercalcemia.

ai.title: Erythema Nodosum
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis presenting as tender red nodules, often on the shins. It is a reactive skin sign of systemic disease, most commonly infection, sarcoidosis or inflammatory bowel disease.

sections.p: Erythema nodosum is a painful, erythematous subcutaneous nodule, usually on the anterior shins. It is a clinical diagnosis; biopsy confirms septal panniculitis without vasculitis.
b: Tender, erythematous nodules 1–3 cm, often bilateral

sections.p: Severity is judged by systemic symptoms and extent of skin involvement. The most useful scale is the EN severity score (ESS) which counts pain, swelling, fever and systemic signs.
In East Africa, infections dominate. TB, streptococcal pharyngitis, malaria, schistosomiasis, HIV and drug reactions are common triggers.

t.b: Positive indicates TB exposure; a strong reaction supports TB as cause
Look for hilar lymphadenopathy or infiltrates; supports sarcoidosis or TB

sections.p: Patients report sudden, painful shin nodules, often with fever, arthralgia and sometimes uveitis. The nodules are usually symmetrical.
Investigations aim to find the underlying cause and rule out complications. In low‑resource settings, focus on simple, affordable tests.

t.b: Anemia or leukocytosis suggests infection or chronic disease
Elevated indicates inflammation; useful when specific tests are unavailable
Positive indicates HIV; may alter management

sections.p: Complications are rare but include severe systemic illness, ocular involvement, and, rarely, necrotizing fasciitis if ulceration occurs.
b: Ocular inflammation – uveitis requires ophthalmology referral
Severe pain with swelling – consider cellulitis
Rapidly enlarging nodules – think necrotizing fasciitis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Supportive care includes analgesia, rest and leg elevation. Avoid NSAIDs if renal disease or bleeding risk.
b: NSAIDs for pain (avoid if renal impairment)

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 4–6 weeks. Prevent recurrence by treating infections promptly and avoiding known drug triggers.
b: Repeat CBC and ESR after treatment
Educate on early treatment of sore throats

sections.p: Differential includes cellulitis, erythema multiforme, and subcutaneous abscesses.
b: Cellulitis – skin warmth, erythema, systemic signs, responds to antibiotics

sections.p: A normal chest X‑ray does not exclude sarcoidosis; a negative Mantoux can miss TB in immunosuppressed patients.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with swelling suggesting cellulitis

faq.q: Can EN be a sign of pregnancy complications?
faq.a: Yes, it can occur in hyperemesis gravidarum or preeclampsia, but these are rare.
No, biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations or when diagnosis is uncertain.

faq.q: Does EN resolve on its own?
faq.a: Often it resolves within 6–8 weeks once the trigger is treated.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with EN in a low‑resource setting? — CBC and ESR to assess inflammation and rule out anemia or infection.
How would you differentiate EN from cellulitis at the bedside? — EN nodules are tender but not warm, no systemic sepsis, and do not improve with antibiotics.
A patient with EN has a positive Mantoux but normal chest X‑ray. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Tuberculosis, possibly miliary or extrapulmonary.
Why is NSAID use cautioned in EN patients with renal disease? — NSAIDs can worsen renal function and increase bleeding risk.
What is the significance of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in a patient with EN? — Suggests sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome) or TB.
If a patient with EN develops sudden visual loss, what is the urgent step? — Immediate ophthalmology referral for possible uveitis.
